drapeaux.note: The French calls Stangneth's book by its German title only; the English edition title “Eichmann Before Jerusalem” was added in parentheses in the body on first occurrence, following the rule for foreign-language titles. In the body, the subtitle of Arendt's book is given as the original English title, Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil, where the French gives a French rendering.

accroche: The phrase is Arendt's. Neither its meaning nor the case it rested on survived intact.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1961, Hannah Arendt attends the trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, one of the organizers of the deportation of the Jews of Europe. She draws from it a book in 1963, whose subtitle has made its way in the world: *Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil*.

Three things, in this order: what she argued, what has been made of it, and what we know today.

## What Arendt Argued

Arendt expected to find a monster. She describes a dull man, concerned with his own advancement, speaking in ready-made phrases. Her diagnosis does not say that evil is ordinary, or excusable. It says that this particular man seemed incapable of thinking, in the sense of picturing another person's point of view.

The German word she uses is *Gedankenlosigkeit*, the absence of thought. Her thesis: crimes of unheard-of scale can be committed without a demonic motive, by people who carry out orders, adjust to the language available and do not ask themselves the question. Banality describes the criminal, never the crime.

## What Has Been Made of It

The expression has been turned into a convenient formula: “anyone could have done it,” even “we are all potential Eichmanns.” Arendt did not write that and explicitly rejected it. She maintained that Eichmann was responsible and had to be tried; she never pleaded circumstances.

The irony is that the formula now serves to excuse, whereas Arendt used it to deny the criminal the tragic grandeur in which he might have draped himself.

## What We Have Known Since

Rigor demands one more step. In 2011, the philosopher Bettina Stangneth publishes *Eichmann vor Jerusalem* (*Eichmann Before Jerusalem*), based on documents that had remained unused, notably the interviews conducted in Argentina by the Dutch journalist Willem Sassen, in which Eichmann speaks without watching himself.

The portrait is entirely different: a convinced antisemite, proud of his role, with an articulate political vision. Stangneth argues that the mediocrity displayed at the trial was a defense strategy, performed before a court, and that Arendt let herself be taken in by it.

## What This Shifts

Two questions must then be separated. Was Eichmann the man without thought described by Arendt? Recent work answers no. Does the concept keep its value for understanding how bureaucracies commit the irreparable? The discussion continues, and many think so, but now detached from the case that gave it its name.

A concept can survive the refutation of its example. It is uncomfortable, and more common than one imagines.

repere.texte: In 2011, working from the interviews Eichmann gave in Argentina to the journalist Willem Sassen, Bettina Stangneth describes a convinced antisemite, proud of his role, and argues that the mediocrity displayed at the trial was a defense strategy.

carte.punch: “The banality of evil” does not mean “anyone could have done it.”
carte.idee: Arendt was targeting the absence of thought in one particular man, not a universal excuse. She always maintained that Eichmann had to be tried. And in 2011, Bettina Stangneth shows, with documents in hand, a convinced ideologue who played at mediocrity at the trial.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Short, and precise on the most widespread misreading.

quiz.question: What exactly did “banality” designate in Arendt?
choix: The ordinary character of the criminal, not that of the crime itself
The statistical frequency of mass crimes in recent history
The fact that such crimes end up no longer shocking public opinion
The idea that everyone would commit the same acts in the same circumstances
quiz.explication: Arendt described Eichmann, not the crime, whose enormity she never minimized. She explicitly rejected the “anyone could have done it” reading and maintained that he had to be tried. Let us add that the work of Bettina Stangneth (2011) has since largely undone the portrait on which she relied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What German word does Arendt use to designate what she observes in Eichmann?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The word Arendt uses is Gedankenlosigkeit, the absence of thought: her thesis is that immense crimes can be committed by people unable to picture another person's point of view.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Arendt explicitly reject, despite the common use made of her formula?
choix: That Eichmann's trial be held publicly in Jerusalem rather than elsewhere
The publication of her book under this precise subtitle, judged provocative
The distinction between the crime committed and the criminal who carried it out
The idea that anyone could have committed the same acts, an excuse for the criminal
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Arendt explicitly rejected the reading that sees in her formula a universal excuse: she always maintained that Eichmann was responsible and had to be tried, without pleading circumstances.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what documents does Bettina Stangneth rely in 2011 to draw an entirely different portrait of Eichmann?
choix: The official minutes of the Jerusalem trial
Letters exchanged with his family during his time on the run
The interviews conducted in Argentina by the journalist Willem Sassen
A private diary found after his death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Stangneth relies on the interviews conducted in Argentina by the Dutch journalist Willem Sassen, in which Eichmann speaks without watching himself, revealing a convinced antisemite proud of his role.
